sweep_summary: Two title hits, both by Harold Crook and both about Nez Perce word stress. (1) Crook 1999 UCLA dissertation: no open full text exists (ProQuest/UMI 9940534 only; UCLA list has no PDF; eScholarship/WorldCat 403, archive.org/Google Books/OATD/CORE empty); its DAI abstract, saved from the Glottolog record, states regular penultimate stress via Non-Finality over Edgemost-Right, long-vowel shortening when unstressed, exceptional classes, and a Sanskrit/Salish-type competition of accented stems, prefixes and suffixes for primary stress -- confirms the 'lexical' coding; priority high to acquire (Harvard has online access per WISHLIST_ACCESS). (2) Crook 1996 (Glottolog 1995) Hokan-Penutian Workshop paper, eScholarship, already held by the project: the 2026-09-16 note that the scan was truncated was wrong -- the file holds the complete paper pp. 1-14 plus Report 9 front matter (copyright 1996; Contents lists Crook at p. 1); pp. It states first-hand that regular nouns take penultimate stress shifting right under light suffixes, that long vowels surface only there, and that a residue of nouns has lexically fixed stress; confirms the catalog, and should be cited directly for the penult default instead of only via Kiparsky 2021/Bjorkman 2010. Aoki 1965 remains the deciding source for the phonemic/lexical status of stress. look-ups were done by automated download against Glottolog, eScholarship GraphQL, ProQuest, archive.org, Google Books, Crossref and the UCLA site.

new_statements.reading: Default word stress is penultimate and re-computed on the inflected word (shifts right under light suffixes); underlying long vowels surface only under penultimate stress; a lexical residue of nouns has stress fixed on a specified syllable regardless of length or position. This is the catalog's 'lexical accent with default penult' coding stated first-hand by the specialist on Nez Perce stress, in an open source. Crook 1999 (abstract read) says the same for the whole language including an accent competition among stems, prefixes and suffixes.

new_statements.relation_note: No placement statement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's 'lexical accent with default penult' coding (Crook 1996). It is compatible with it and adds domain detail: one stress per word including compounds, stress is a lexical property written on every entry, stems fall into stressed and unstressed classes that condition suffix allomorphs, and a set of particles is unstressed. Aoki's examples wé·cese / we·cé·se and the 'stressed stem' vs 'unstressed stem' distinction agree with the lexical-accent side of the catalog reading; the dictionary says nothing about a penultimate default.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary gives no rule for where word stress falls. It says only that stress exists and is written with the acute on every entry (its two examples put the stress on different syllables of near-identical shapes, wé·cese vs we·cé·se, so the mark carries lexical information), that a word, including a compound, carries one stress, that several particles are unstressed or rarely stressed, and that some suffixes have different shapes after stressed and unstressed stems. Placement itself must be read off the individual headwords, which are all accented.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The one explicit statement about stress count is that a compound containing cilim 'has only one stress' (p. 641).
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed or variably stressed words, all particles or bound forms: ča'noʔ 'that person' — 'This word is not stressed' (p. 60); ʔiske/ʔiski 'like, as if' — 'This word is not stressed' (p. 1078); taxc 'soon, now' — 'It is rarely stressed' (p. 695); ʔimet (inferential particle) — 'The stem is unstressed unless it is lengthened as ʔimé·t' (p. 1026); kuʔ 'perhaps' — 'This particle may be either unstressed or stressed' (p. 256); the suffix -hi·n 'having' is listed as 'hi·n (with stress)' and 'hin (without stress)' (p. 149); mé·y 'morning' — 'In nonfinal position and when stressed, mé·y alternates with mé·' (p. 438). Stress-conditioned allomorphy: plural i vs i· after stressed vs unstressed stems (p. 183); passive participle in / iʔs after a stressed s-class stem vs yi·n / ʔi·n after an unstressed one (p. 186); completive naqi after a c-class stem or an s-class stem ending in a stressed vowel vs tnaqi otherwise (p. 468).
new_statements.identity_note: Aoki states (p. ix) that 'Most of the material in this dictionary represents the Upriver Dialect of the Kamiah and Lapwai area'; the Downriver differences he lists (extra labiovelar consonant, o/u merger, no vowel harmony, š for s, l for n) are segmental only, with nothing said about stress in either dialect. Crook 1996 (existing statement) describes the same Upriver-based standard variety recorded by Aoki.

sources.quote: "Stress in Nez Perce depends on the interaction between default alignment preferences and underlying accents (i.e. lexically determined stresses). The default pattern is for primary stress to be rightmost in some domain." Sec. 2.1: "in the absence of other determining factors primary stress in Nez Perce is aligned at the right edge of the word: stress is regularly penultimate (rather than absolutely final), and shifts rightwards under suffixation" (pískis / pìskísne, wéeptes / wèptéesne); secondary stress on initial syllables; sec. 2.2: morphemes with lexical accents keep primary stress fixed

sources.quote: p.1: "In Nez Perce, by far the majority of nouns obey regular principles of stress assignment. Nevertheless, there is a considerable residue of nouns with unpredictable stress under some or all grammatical inflections." p.2: "(1) a. Morphology: Stress placement respects certain morphological principles. b. Weight to Stress: Place stress on a long vowel if there is one. c. Non-Finality: Do not place stress on the final syllable. d. Rightmost syllable: Place stress as close as possible to the word's right edge." fn.7 p.7: "the initial vowel has the highest pitch and is slightly lengthened, the most consistent phonetic correlate of main stress in Nez Perce."

sources.quote: I account for the regular penultimate form of Nez Perce stress, in terms of the interaction of Non-Finality and Edgemost Right. Weight to Stress requires that underlying long vowels be shortened when do not receive main stress. To this basic pattern must be added a set of words where Non-Finality is outranked by Edgemost Right, and a set where long vowels are blocked from shortening. Nez Perce has a robust accentual system akin to Sanskrit and Salish, where accented stems, prefixes, and suffixes all compete to receive primary stress. I also provide accounts for compound stress, secondary stress, stress driven epenthesis, and syncope.
sources.locator: DAI-A 60/08 p. 2890 abstract (jsondata.abstract in the Glottolog record)
sources.note: The only full-length primary description of Nez Perce stress (default penult, accent competition, weight-sensitive secondary stress ch. 4, pp. 290-445); our positional rule and secondary-stress/weight fields cite its pages only through Kiparsky 2021 and Bjorkman 2010.
